content: Sterile pyuria is defined as the persistent presence of white blood cells in the urine without detectable bacteria, as determined by aerobic culture techniques using a 5% sheep-blood agar plate and a MacConkey agar plate. Pyuria itself refers to the presence of 10 or more white blood cells per cubic millimeter in a urine sample, three or more white blood cells per high-power field in unspun urine, a positive Gram’s stain of unspun urine, or a positive leukocyte esterase result on a urinary dipstick test. Bacteriuria, on the other hand, is characterized by bacterial colony counts exceeding 1000 colony-forming units (CFU) per milliliter in urine. The causes of sterile pyuria can be categorized into infectious and non-infectious etiologies. Infectious causes include: Gynecologic infections. Urethritis caused by pathogens such as Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Mycoplasma species, or Ureaplasma species. Prostatitis. Balanitis. Appendicitis. Viral infections of the lower genitourinary tract. Genitourinary tuberculosis. Fungal infections. Parasitic diseases, such as trichomoniasis or schistosomiasis. Non-infectious causes include: Current use of antibiotics. A recently treated urinary tract infection (within the past two weeks). The presence or recent use of a urinary catheter. Recent cystoscopy or urologic endoscopy. Urinary tract stones. Foreign bodies, such as surgical mesh in the urethra or a retained stent. Urinary tract neoplasms. Pelvic irradiation. Urinary fistulas. Polycystic kidney disease. Rejection of a renal transplant. Renal vein thrombosis. Interstitial nephritis or analgesic nephropathy. Papillary necrosis. Interstitial cystitis. Inflammatory diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus or Kawasaki disease. Pathogen-specific antimicrobial therapies are as follows: 1. Tuberculosis: The preferred regimen includes isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide for 3–6 months. 2. Gonorrhea: The preferred regimen is a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg, followed by either a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g or oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. 3. Chlamydia: The preferred regimen is either a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g or oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. An alternative regimen is erythromycin base 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days. 4. Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma: The preferred regimen includes azithromycin, levofloxacin, or moxifloxacin. 5. Genital Herpes: The preferred regimen includes acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 7–10 days, acyclovir 200 mg orally five times daily for 7–10 days, famciclovir 250 mg orally three times daily for 7–10 days, or valacyclovir 1 g orally twice daily for 7 days. 6. Trichomoniasis: The preferred regimen is either a single oral dose of metronidazole 2 g or tinidazole 2 g. 7. Fungal Infections: The preferred regimen includes fluconazole, posaconazole, echinocandins, or amphotericin B. 8. Schistosomiasis: The preferred regimen is praziquantel 20 mg/kg orally twice daily for 1–2 days.
